citation: "Grant Park (Chicago)." Wikipedia. History of the lakefront park formerly called Lake Park, carrying the Illinois Central causeway, lagoon and fill chronology after Cremin, 'Waterfront', in The Encyclopedia of Chicago (University of Chicago Press, 2004), pp. 864-6.
note: Read 2026-09-17 (action=raw, HTTP 200) for one paragraph, which is the whole reason this record exists and is quoted here so that what the project leans on is visible: 'The city officially designated the land as a park on April 29, 1844, naming it Lake Park. When the Illinois Central Railroad was built into Chicago in 1852, it was permitted to lay track along the lakefront on a causeway built offshore from the park. The resulting lagoon became stagnant, and was largely filled in 1871 with debris from the Great Chicago Fire, increasing the parkland. In 1896, the city began extending the park into the lake with landfill, beyond the rail lines.' That is four dated states of the downtown lake edge, footnoted to Cremin's 'Waterfront' article in the Encyclopedia of Chicago. Its consequence for this project is a NEGATIVE one and it is the useful kind: between 1871 and 1896 the downtown lake edge is the Illinois Central causeway with filled ground behind it, and it does not move. So the whole of the 1880s is ONE lakefront state, the choice of a representative year inside the decade cannot be decided on the lake edge, and the modern Grant Park and Museum Campus fill - all of it 1896 and later - is out of the epoch by a quarter-century. IT IS A DOWNTOWN READING AND IT IS NOT A PRAIRIE AVENUE READING: Lake Park lay between Randolph and what is now Roosevelt Road, and Prairie Avenue's blocks are a mile further south. Nothing here says where the Illinois Central ran at 18th Street or where the water stood off it, and this record must not be stretched to say so. The source to chase for that: Cremin, 'Waterfront', pp. 864-6, and the fire-insurance and lakefront-survey mapping the successor trace ticket owns.
